Record of the Installation of the Sacred Image of Amitābha in the Xiangguang Chamber: An Exposition of the Record [The following is a translation of the title and introductory section: **Record of the Installation of the Sacred Image of Amitābha in the Xiangguang Chamber: An Exposition of the Record** In the year of the Great Qing, the 10th year of Jiaqing (1805), the first month, the fifteenth day, a sacred image of the Buddha Amitābha was enshrined within the Xiangguang Chamber at the Yunju Monastery in the capital. This record sets forth the circumstances of its establishment and the principles underlying its veneration, intended to serve as a perpetual testament for future generations. It is said that the Tathāgata Amitābha, through his vows of great compassion, established the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the Western Quarter, wherein all who aspire with sincerity shall be reborn. To manifest this truth and provide a focal point for the faithful, this sacred image was commissioned. Its features are sublime: the countenance is serene and majestic, the body is radiant and luminous, and it is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. It is crafted from precious materials, imbued with spiritual power, and capable of responding to the prayers of sentient beings. The chamber where it is enshrined is named "Xiangguang" (Fragrant Light). This name signifies that the light of the Buddha’s wisdom permeates all things, purifying the minds of those who encounter it and dispelling the darkness of ignorance. Within this space, practitioners may cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, recite his name, and contemplate his pure land, thereby accumulating merit and advancing toward liberation. This record is written to ensure that the significance of this installation is not forgotten and that the practice of venerating the Buddha Amitābha continues without decline. May all who see, hear, or touch this image be inspired to take refuge in the Three Jewels and attain birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. [End of introductory section]

Affection cannot be bound and resentment cannot be hidden; driving away the crows, I sigh in the rhyme of Gao Rui-nan, on the occasion of the eightieth birthday of Layman Shen Guangshan, with a preface for the *Nirvāṇa Hall*. [Preface] Layman Shen Guangshan is a man of profound virtue and vast learning. He has long cultivated his mind in the Way and has extensively practiced the teachings of the Buddha. At the age of eighty, he has retired to the Nirvāṇa Hall to dwell in quietude. I, your humble servant, have composed this poem to celebrate his longevity and to express my admiration for his steadfast resolve. May his life be as enduring as the eternal Dharma, and may he continue to illuminate the world with the light of wisdom. *The following is the poem in the rhyme of Gao Rui-nan:* In the deep stillness of the Nirvāṇa Hall, The fragrant breeze carries the scent of incense. The moonlight shines upon the ancient pine, And the dew falls softly upon the lotus pond. His spirit is as vast as the open sky, His heart is as clear as a mirror’s surface. For eighty years he has lived in harmony, Never once allowing worldly passions to bind him. Though the years have passed and his hair has turned white, His inner radiance remains undiminished. I sigh that the bird of sorrow must be driven away, For here, in this hall of liberation, there is no room for grief. May you live a hundred autumns, And forever propagate the True Dharma. I offer these words in praise, To honor the sage who dwells in peace. [End of Poem]

In the end, it all returns to the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, the aforementioned three methods may be condensed into two: first, visualization; second, the recitation of the name.
Regarding visualization, the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations* explains it in great detail. As for this discussion on the recitation of the name, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"Upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, one should hold fast to that name. Whether for one day, two days, or even..."
Upon reaching the seventh day, with a single mind free from distraction, at the time of that person’s passing, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
This is the great original source from which the ten-thousand-year practice of *nianfo* by reciting the name has emerged; it is the word of the Golden Mouth.
This is the sublime Dharma proclaimed by those we hold dear. An ancient virtuous master said: "The principles of the Dharma are subtle, while the minds of sentient beings are杂 (mixed/confused).
When one cultivates contemplation with a confused mind, the visualization is difficult to perfect. Out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorted us to single-mindedly uphold the Name.

This is because the act of reciting the Name is easy; through continuous practice, rebirth occurs. This explains that the merit of *nianfo* by upholding the Name is the most effective means for rebirth in the Pure Land."
This is the essential point regarding the earth. If one holds the Name and deeply penetrates the true aspect (*dharmatā*), its efficacy will be equal to that of wondrous contemplation;

there is no doubt that one will be reborn in the highest of the high grades. O present sons of the Buddha, as in the previous section on the gate of repentance, even the noble ones of the two vehicles [attain this].

This is because this Dharma-door of Buddha-remembrance makes no distinction between male or female, monastic or lay, nor between noble or humble, wise or foolish; provided one maintains single-mindedness without distraction, one will attain birth in the nine grades according to the magnitude of one's meritorious practice.

People, you must urgently recite the Buddha’s name. You shall attain rebirth in the nine grades of the Pure Land. Upon the blossoming of the lotus flower, you will behold the Buddha; having beheld the Buddha and heard the Dharma, you will ultimately achieve Buddhahood.

A Universal Exhortation to Practice Buddha-Recitation: Now, for those who study the Buddha-dharma, it matters not whether they adorn their outward appearance; what is valued above all is authentic practice.

Lay practitioners need not necessarily don black robes or clerical caps; those who retain their hair may naturally continue to wear their ordinary clothes while constantly reciting the Buddha’s name. It is not required.

One must strike the fish-bell and beat the drum. Those who prefer tranquility may simply remain silent and recite the Buddha’s name; there is no need to insist on forming groups for communal assemblies.
Those who fear worldly affairs may simply close their doors and recite the Buddha’s name; there is no need to insist on entering temples to listen to sutras.
Those who can read may simply recite the Buddha’s name according to the teachings. Rather than burning incense at a distance of a thousand li, it is better to sit peacefully in one's own place.

Reciting the Buddha’s name while maintaining a domestic altar and serving heterodox teachers is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name with filial piety toward one's parents. Associating extensively with demonic friends is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name alone in purity.
Making offerings for future lives by depositing funds in a merit storehouse is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name while performing meritorious deeds in the present life.
To seek protection through making vows and performing exorcisms is not as good as repenting one's faults, renewing oneself, and reciting the Buddha’s name.

To study the texts of non-Buddhist paths is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name without knowing even a single character. To speak recklessly of the principles of Chan out of ignorance is not as good as sincerely upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name.
To seek supernatural powers from malevolent spirits and ghosts is not as good as upholding right faith in cause and effect and reciting the Buddha’s name. To speak of the essentials:

to rectify the mind and extinguish evil while thus reciting the Buddha’s name is called being a "good person. To restrain the mind and eliminate distraction while thus reciting the Buddha’s name is called being a "worthy person.
To awaken the mind and sever delusions while thus reciting the Buddha’s name is called being a "sage."

Furthermore, he exhorted those who were extremely leisurely to practice *nien-fo*. He said that once their marriages were complete and their descendants were capable of managing the household, they would be at peace and free from affairs;
this was precisely the time to devote their whole hearts and full strength to reciting the Buddha’s name, chanting several thousand times each day, even up to tens of thousands.
First, I exhort those who are half-busy and half-leisurely to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Whether they are busy or at leisure—though not entirely free from affairs—they may attend to their duties during busy times and recite the Buddha’s name during leisure times. Each day, they should recite several hundred or even several thousand times.

First, I exhort those who are extremely busy to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name. Even for those exhausted by official duties or the frantic toil of household affairs—who, though having no leisure time—must nevertheless steal moments from their busyness to recite the Buddha’s name.
Every morning at dawn, they should perform ten recitations; during the day as well, they may recite several hundred times.
An Essential Discourse on Reading the Tripitaka:
That which is expounded in the Great Tripitaka does not exceed the precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Nevertheless, there are two kinds of faults in those who read the Tripitaka:
first, clinging to the literal words while remaining deluded regarding the underlying principles; second, understanding the principles while failing to realize the mind. In vain...

To waste one’s time merely serves to create the seeds of karmic conditions. If one can realize and penetrate the cultivation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, then the teachings of the entire Tripitaka will be ever-present in every thought-moment;
this is what it means to be mindful of hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls of scripture in each instant.

Furthermore, one should recognize that this very practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is itself the gate of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Why is this so? "Precept" has the meaning of preventing what is wrong.
If one can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, no evils will dare to enter; this is precisely the precept. "Concentration" has the meaning of removing distraction.
If one single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, the mind does not wander toward other objects; this is precisely concentration. "Wisdom" has the meaning of luminous illumination. If...
Contemplate the Buddha’s voice; each syllable is distinct and clear. Furthermore, contemplate that both the one who recollects and the object recollected are ungraspable—this is wisdom (*prajñā*).

To practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner is itself the cultivation of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Why must one merely follow the text and pursue each individual word while reading this Tripitaka?
Time passes swiftly; life is not enduring. I pray that all people shall regard pure karma as their urgent task, and by no means disregard my words as being false or fail to listen to them.

He showed that for the two groups of laypeople—sons and mothers, husbands and wives, and all members of a single family—their being gathered together for a time is entirely due to causes and conditions from past lives;
they must inevitably part in the end, so there is no reason for grief or suffering. What is truly lamentable and pitiable is to have spent one's entire life in vain.
Simply recite the Buddha’s name. Now, merely set down all myriad conditions and turn the light back upon itself to recite the Buddha’s name;

In this recitation, each syllable must be reflected upon by the mind, making it vivid and distinct. At every moment, apply the mind with earnestness, allowing not even the slightest bit of delusive thought to intermingle.
Reflect: whenever you pay homage to the Buddha in the morning or evening, make a sincere and earnest vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the instruction for the sick, there is an ancient saying: "Illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings. Therefore, when one is ill, one should give rise to great joy;

While ill, you should give rise to great liberation; accept death and life as they come, and do not harbor fear.
Furthermore, the past is like an illusion, the present is like an illusion, and the future is like an illusion. Relinquish everything with total sincerity, maintaining nothing but right mindfulness.
During your illness, exercise patience and composure by all means; do not harbor a restless desire for a swift recovery. This is precisely the excellent remedy for a quick recovery.
Furthermore,
having settled all household affairs and cast aside all worldly concerns, with a mind that is utterly empty, one should recite only the six characters.
If one does not forget the name of the Buddha for even a moment, karmic obstacles will naturally be extinguished.

I have shown that while the physical body of an elderly lay practitioner naturally undergoes decline and frailty, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is fundamentally without retrogression or extinction.

By exhausting all myriad burdens and purifying the single mind—whereby the purification of the mind leads to the purification of the land—one achieves rebirth; yet through this, the realization of non-arising is spontaneously attained.

although the physical forms of male and female differ, the nature of spiritual luminosity is non-dual. Why speak of the five outflows? One values only the single mind.
Single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha, and you will certainly be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

This demonstrates that, like the ancients, one should draw near to an enlightened teacher and seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, such a spiritual friend truly possesses no oral transmission of the mind.
The secret dharma-gate is simply to untie the adhesions and remove the bonds for others; this is what constitutes the secret.
Now, merely to uphold the name with a single mind without distraction—these eight characters are themselves the secret dharma-gate that unties adhesions and removes bonds.
This is the grand, open highway for transcending birth and death. Whether recollecting in the morning or evening, while walking or sitting, let your mindfulness continue from moment to moment;
you will spontaneously attain samādhi—do not seek it elsewhere.

Furthermore, when a mind long accustomed to distraction is suddenly difficult to stabilize, do not worry if the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is not yet clear; it simply requires that your practice be deep.
You should attend to every word and every phrase with focused mindfulness.
I show the King that when the mind is empty, karma is empty; when the body is empty, illness is empty. If you have any lingering doubts, you may let them go entirely. As the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena that possess marks are but false and illusory. Since they belong to the realm of the false and illusory, they are like flowers in the sky or bubbles upon the water.

It is like a matter occurring in a dream; what cause for doubt could there be? Diminish discursive thought, restrain vexation and anger, moderate your food and drink, and be careful in your daily conduct.
At all times and at every moment, take the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) as your *huatou* (critical phrase).
Do not allow it to be forgotten, and you will maintain constant awareness and illumination, remaining alert and never deluded.
The Master Shiming noted that excessive counting and overly tightening the mind cause various ailments; one should simply practice with diligent and subtle consistency, without interruption.

Freedom from admixture is itself the practice; there is no need for excessive asceticism. When delusive thoughts become stubborn, they will submit naturally after a long struggle—of this there is no doubt.

Do not concern yourself with whether there is awakening or not; do not concern yourself with existence, non-existence, internal, external, or the middle; do not concern yourself with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
do not concern yourself with whether this dharma-gate is the same as or different from other dharma-gates. Since doubt has not arisen, do not concern yourself with who is right and who is wrong.
Whoever merely upholds the name with single-mindedness and focused intent, practicing it continuously and without interruption in a state of pure, undivided concentration—Guanghui once said:
"Discursive thoughts are the disease;
mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicine. Mindfulness of the Buddha directly treats discursive thoughts; yet, [if one lacks this focus], one cannot cure them.

This means that one must be diligent in mindfulness without distraction. When distracted thoughts arise, apply the mind with effort to recite the Buddha’s name, making each word and every phrase singular and undivided;
then, distracting thoughts will naturally subside.

I show the King that the grand mansion is not as good as directly grasping and holding onto a single phrase: "Amitābha Buddha. Recite it with all your heart and all your strength, without even a hair’s breadth of divergent thought;
this is precisely the "Mu" (No) kōan. There is no need to bring up other koans such as "Mu"; simply [recite this].
A single thought of the Buddha penetrates the Buddha; it penetrates through a thousand places and ten thousand locations.

To Wu Guangshou:
Since you do not doubt birth and death, nor do you doubt the public cases (gongan) of the ancient masters, how can you give rise to great fear? How can you still harbor such [doubts]?
This refers to the apprehension that the arrow of doubt has entered one's heart. That which is called "being without doubt" still implies the presence of doubt.

In the past, two bhikṣus committed the offenses of sexual misconduct and killing; yet under a single word from Vimalakīrti, their transgressions were extinguished without remainder. If you can now act as those two bhikṣus did, [you shall likewise be liberated].

This need not be discussed further. Otherwise, there is another method. A sutra states: "Reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart even once extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
If one recites the Buddha’s name with devotion ten thousand and eight thousand times, there is no sin that will not be extinguished."

The spells that were to be punished were like wind sweeping away clouds, like the sun dissolving dew, like a single drop cast into the great ocean, or like a flake of snow falling upon a red-hot furnace;
they were completely purified and extinguished, leaving no further trace behind.
[The Master] showed this to Lin Rong of Fujian (Rong fully recounted the extraordinary visions he had seen).

The Buddha taught the ten kinds of merit of mindfulness of the Buddha:
if a person upholds the name of even a single Buddha, they shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious benefits in this present life.
First, day and night they will constantly be protected by the great powerful deities and spirits, together with their retinues, who remain hidden from view.
Second, they will always be followed and protected by twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as by all bodhisattvas.
Third, they will always be protected and remembered day and night by all Buddhas; Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit light rays to gather them in and sustain them.
A person [who possesses this] cannot be harmed by any evil spirits, whether yakṣas or rākṣasas. No poisonous snakes, venomous dragons,
or toxic drugs shall be able to cause them harm.
Fifth: All calamities of fire, calamities of water, enemies and bandits, blades and arrows, imprisonment, shackles and fetters, untimely deaths, and unjust deaths—none shall befall them.
Sixth: All previously committed sins shall be completely extinguished; those whose lives were taken as enemies shall attain liberation, and there will be no further resentment or opposition.
Seventh: One’s dreams at night will be upright, or one may dream of the sublime and wondrous physical body of Amitābha Buddha.
8. Their minds are always joyful; their countenances are radiant; their physical strength is abundant; and all they do is auspicious. 9.
They are constantly revered, honored, and prostrated to by all the people of the world, just as one would revere a Buddha.

Tenth: At the time of death, their minds will be free from fear; right mindfulness will manifest before them, and they will behold Amitābha Buddha along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and holy beings.
Holding golden palanquins, these beings will welcome them to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, where they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.
Record of the Installation of a Sacred Image of Amitābha in the Xiangguang Studio.
Yunqi [Zhuhong] enshrined one statue of Amitābha to welcome and guide sentient beings. Layman Benru beheld its dignified form.
It was truly magnificent and beautiful. I commissioned artisans to carve a likeness of it, and as soon as it was completed, my second brother came from Tongcheng to welcome it.
Because the gold lacquer had not yet set, I had it carried by palanquin on the boat, fearing it might be damaged;

thus, we replaced the original image with the new one for the journey, leaving the new image behind in the mountains. My brother escorted the image to the North Gate, intending to purchase a boat, but the boatman—
One night he dreamed of a golden-hued man who requested a ride. Upon waking, he waited for him to arrive, thinking that he must surely be a person of great nobility.
He refused everyone who came to inquire about him; even when Zhongjun asked, he still refused. It was only later that he learned the man possessed a sacred image.
Furthermore, upon examining it closely, they recognized that it was a standing image; they were greatly rejoiced, believing it to be the very one they had dreamed of.

When they reached Jingkou and were about to change boats to enter the Yangtze River, the boatman there again dreamed as before. Before long, the image arrived at their home and was enshrined in the Xiangguang Hall.
Just as they were concerned that there might be no virtuous monk to guard it, a monk named Daida happened to arrive. Daiai was indeed steadfast.
He strictly purified his discipline (*vinaya*), never crossing the threshold of his dwelling for seven years. Foreknowing the time of his departure, he invited the lay devotee to bid him farewell.
On the first day of the seventh month, he passed away while seated. Those who were moved and transformed by him from near and far were exceedingly numerous.
After Hai died, fearing there would be no successor, he obtained Hui-guang; Guang was a worthy companion to Hai. Indeed, it was like a dream for the boatman.
How extraordinary! That these [images] should appear together in a dream—is this not also extraordinary? It was difficult enough to first obtain the Great Ocean;
that it should follow with the Radiance of Wisdom (Prajñā-prabhāsa)—is this not even more difficult? To possess both is something never before encountered.

That which causes this response is the majestic spiritual power (vīrya-tejas) of Amitābha; and that which moves the majestic spiritual power of Amitābha is the lay devotee’s (upāsaka) refined sincerity. *Leng*... [text fragment].

Yan said: "Recalling the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. He further stated: "It is like a person who has been smeared with incense;

Yan now may be said to have seen the Buddha without waiting for the future, as he has already achieved this adornment of fragrant light. Therefore, I have gathered these passages from his earlier and later works and recorded them here.
Regarding the discourse on the skull diagram, Master Fu Dashi said:
"Gradually the skin becomes like that of a rooster and the hair turns as white as a crane; look at how the gait becomes increasingly faltering. Even if one possesses gold and jade,"
The entire hall is filled with those who cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, and death. No matter how many kinds of happiness you may possess, impermanence will inevitably arrive.
There is only the practice of the direct path; simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. These words of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) are precisely what is meant by:
"Of all things, nothing can be taken away; only one's karma follows along. What does it mean that "nothing can be taken away"? It refers to the person.

Regarding all the official ranks and titles, gold and jewels, houses and dwellings, fields and gardens, food and drink, clothing, and articles of pleasure—even including one’s beloved wife and cherished children—when impermanence arrives, which single one of these can be taken along? How is it that only karma follows the person?

Throughout their lives, humans create various karmas of greed, anger, and delusion; they commit improper acts of lewdness and adultery, and they slaughter animals at will according to their own desires.
As a son, you oppose your father; as a minister, you deceive your sovereign; you amass wealth at the expense of the multitude and harbor malice toward all living beings.
Amidst such various evil karmas, when impermanence arrives, these will all follow you closely.

Since this is so, if you do not wake up with urgency and turn back, reforming your evils for the sake of goodness and cleansing your mind through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, will it not be that you have obtained a human body in vain and lived a life of empty death?
Alas, alas! When I observe the people of this world, each and every one of them wishes to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Now, I shall categorize them into three types. First are those who are extremely free from worldly affairs; they ought to practice single-minded Buddha-remembrance day and night. Second are those who are half-free and half-busy;
they ought to practice Buddha-remembrance immediately once their business affairs are concluded. Third are those who are extremely busy; they ought to [practice] amidst their busyness...

To steal a moment of leisure and recite the Buddha’s name ten times. Furthermore, those who are wealthy and noble, with abundant clothing and sustenance, are precisely the ones who should best practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Those who are poor and destitute, living in contentment and adhering to their lot, are precisely the ones who should best practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Those who have children and grandchildren, having others to take over their labors, [should likewise do so].
It is precisely the right time for those without descendants to practice nianfo, as their minds are free from attachments.

It is precisely the right time for those who are not ill to practice nianfo, as their physical strength is healthy and robust. It is precisely the right time for those who are ill to practice nianfo, as they know death will not be long in coming.

Those who are intelligent and wise, who have mastered the scriptures and understood the principles, are precisely those who should practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*). Those who are dull and slow-witted, who lack diverse and confused knowledge and views, are precisely those who should practice the Buddha-remembrance.
To speak of the essentials: throughout the heavens and the human realm, across the four modes of birth and the nine states of existence, all should practice the Buddha-remembrance.
I exhort all people of the world: Why not take advantage of this time, while these four elements have not yet become a skull, and practice the Buddha’s name early?
Wait until nothing can be taken with you at all, and only karma follows you; by then, it will be too late for regret.

Eulogy for the Portrait of Layman Yu of Langu Valley:

"I am as emaciated as withered firewood and as decayed as fallen leaves. My mouth is like that of a blind turtle, and my clumsiness is equal to that of a lame tortoise. I have no Way to honor."
There are no dharmas that can be spoken of. When asked why he sits in the lotus posture, he simply recites the name of Amitābha Buddha.
The meaning of this verse cannot be contradicted.
Two hearts first shared in joy, Bound by a covenant as firm as metal and stone. Yet in a single day, misfortune arose;
In their abandonment, they were like discarded objects. Alas! Such bestial minds— While ghosts and spirits watched from their side, They failed to see the descendant of Han.
Thus, with earnest longing, he sought his "old sword," Unmoved by the pull of new affections.
Suddenly causing old attachments to vanish, Both new and old alike return to emptiness. When will this great dream end?
I vow that throughout this very life, We may together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
Such kindness must never be forgotten.
A man of vigor possesses a resolute heart; he does not forget the repayment for a single meal. How much more so for one who knows the Way—how could he bear to act as a deceitful man?
When in peril, one relies on another’s support; yet once it passes before his eyes, he looks away. Try reflecting on this during a quiet night:
would you not feel ashamed and break into a sweat? Throughout your life, have you truly been a man?
Constantly examine yourself within your own heart; Ultimately, realize this debt of gratitude. Together ascend to the shore of Ultimate Bliss;
Sentiment should not be bound by antiquity.
The friendship of the noble man is described as vast and serene as water; It is not that his feelings are merely sparse.
The vision of the Path is thus: the Illustrious Emperor attained the Great Truth. Who could compare lacquer and glue to this?
At the post station of Ma’wei, my heart was wounded; since that single parting, a thousand years have passed. Where does such affection now remain?
Like empty flowers, beauty before the eyes is but a delusion; alas, from time immemorial, the tears of separation have flowed across the four seas.
Great suffering is forever cast aside, as all return together to the assembly of Ultimate Bliss.

Yuan Ang killed Chao Cuo, Thus creating a grievance that lasts for a thousand ages. Had it not been for Yuan Ang’s stratagem, [the disaster would have been avoided].
How could error endure for long? The great destiny is not of human making; it is the Unseen that causes it thus.
The four elements undergo birth and death of their own accord—what concern is this to me? O Sage, the Yellow-Faced Elder!
Before you, even the value of a needle or a blade is treated with a smile. Enemies and kin are fundamentally equal; together we shall roam the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Driving away the crows, one sighs at the clamor of ten thousand trees; The fine birds have ceased their songs, Harmed by their cruel pecking, more pitiless than the snare.
Though one’s body is beneath the *kāṣāya*, Can one not harbor thoughts of compassion?
Alas for this forest of turbid evil! I vow to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.

When will your afflictions end? I know you have given rise to great wisdom. Your mind is like wood already withered;
having leaped out from the barrier of drunken dreams, who would say the West is remote? I ask:

*An Inscription for the Nirvāṇa Hall (with Preface)* Chan Master Zhenxie Liao composed a single regulated verse on the Nirvāṇa Hall. It is poignant and piercing, moving one to sorrow.

Original composition.
Visiting old friends and reflecting on the past truly brings sorrow;
For years I have lain alone in the Nirvana Hall—no guests pass by the door, no paper at the window, Cold ashes remain in the brazier, and frost settles upon my mat.
Only after falling ill do I realize that the body is suffering; In my health, I was mostly busy for the sake of others.
This old monk has his own way of peace and ease; Though the eight sufferings press upon him all at once, he is not hindered.
Now, with this illusory body, who knows of decay or injury? Lifting his head, he is startled and falls prostrate in the Hall of Nirvana.
A lifetime is exhausted as the final watch of the night fades; ten thousand anxieties turn to ash like the frost upon a bright sun.

Now you wish to inquire about the Dharma of peace and ease, but digging a pond when already thirsty is too late.

Body and mind cast off, free from reliance and beyond injury, The chronic ailment is gone; all day long one stands with natural dignity.
The lamp of mind destroys darkness, as bright as the moon; The sword of wisdom subdues demons, as stern as frost.
When medicine and illness are both non-existent, what is there to debate? Since birth and death are both illusions, there is no need for haste.

A village man who could not recognize a single character had, upon a fleeting thought, caused even ghosts to show him reverence; how much more so for one who has practiced for a long time? Therefore, the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha—
Their virtue is inconceivable.

They take suffering to be pleasure, like the insects in a latrine. From the perspective of dogs or sheep, that place would be unbearable in its misery; yet the insects therein do not perceive it as such.

At first, I doubted this, wondering how it could be that Śrāvakas, who already possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), and Bodhisattvas, who cultivate both meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), should both be so clouded and fail to escape these states. Upon further investigation...
Reflecting upon myself and others, the events of last night suddenly vanished at dawn; how much more so when separated by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
When one first moves to a new room and rises in the night, one does not even know north from south; how much more so when emerging from the womb?
The confusion experienced by those noble sages was but a temporary obscuration followed by immediate clarity, a momentary dullness followed by gradual awakening; yet as for us ordinary beings—
In the end, one becomes muddled and unconscious of this. From the casting off of one body to the taking up of another, the stakes of gain and loss are such as these.
As for your current plan, you must simply remain firm and concentrated in your right mind, ensuring that not even for a single kṣaṇa do you lose your illumination.

Furthermore, you must earnestly and sincerely seek rebirth in the Pure Land; once reborn in the Pure Land, such muddled unconsciousness will be no cause for concern. Having already allowed your mind to wander, you must now...
To cast aside the Pure Land—how perilous this is!
When Lü Wenzheng Gong rose each morning to prostrate before the Buddha, he would offer this prayer: "May those who do not believe in the Triple Gem never be born in my land."
The family prayed that their descendants might enjoy official stipends for generations and protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Later, those born of the Lü clan—whether it be Gongzhu, Hao Wen, or Yongzhong—all attained high status and prominence while serving the Buddha. Now, Wen Zheng was merely an ordinary man;

yet his virtuous vow was ultimately fulfilled as expected, continuing unbroken through successive generations. How much more so, then, for those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land, which is the ultimate goal!
This is the great vow of the world. As for the vow of Wen Zheng, which sought certainty through his descendants—whether it would be fulfilled or not remains unknown.
How much more so, then, when seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, where one must seek certainty within oneself?

Thus we know that the Pure Land is not realized precisely because one’s sincerity has not reached its ultimate limit. Formerly, there was a noble family who supported a monk. They asked the monk, "Master..."
"After a hundred years, will you be willing to come to my house? The monk smiled and subsequently became his son.
This is precisely analogous to the case of the contemporary military commander, Mr. Fan, who was also a monk supported by his father; these two instances are exactly alike.

Indeed, if a momentary smile and a word of agreement can lead one to become a member of a noble family, how could long-accumulated sincerity fail to find rebirth within the lotus rank? Cause and effect are certain.
Indeed, there is no room for further deliberation.

Among those in the nine grades who attain rebirth in the Land, there are some who hold the Pure Land in low esteem and do not practice; they say, "Just like our own class, one ought to enter [the world] through official rank."
[The official] replied, "I serve as an official. How can I accept an office by way of the annual tribute system?
A local man said, "This analogy is a great error. The lotus pedestal itself is divided into nine grades. Why do you not take the highest, but instead settle for a lower grade?
Today, there are three hundred 'lotus scholars' (lianshi); these too may be divided into upper, middle, and lower, thus forming nine grades. Why do you not take the vanguard of them?"
Why then would one willingly place oneself at the very bottom of the list? To be born in the "Highest Rank of the Highest Grade" is to be at the head of the register of the Lotus Section.

Thus, those who praise this state say: "The three minds are fully developed, and the profound principle of truth is clearly realized; one proceeds to the Golden Terrace and immediately realizes non-arising.

In the context of the Chan school, this refers to one who has attained great penetration and great awakening—the so-called "returning home after passing the examination with an empty mind. This is what is meant by being directed toward that land.
The man sighed in dismay and said, "My doubts have been dispelled by this.
From now on, I shall recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten thousand times day and night. (From *Zhūchuāng sānbǐ*).
It is traditionally said that the Great Master Yongming recited the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred thousand times day and night. I once tested this myself:
from the first watch of the current day until the first watch of the following day—completing the full twelve hours and one hundred *ke*—I exactly reached one hundred thousand recitations.

However, those recited were only the four-character name; had they been the six-character name, the total count would not have been reached. This was true even when accounting for the time spent eating, drinking, and relieving oneself.
There must be no interruption; even a brief interval fails to reach the full count. Sleep and speech must both be completely severed;
even a slight lapse fails to reach the full count. Furthermore, if one is rushed and hurried, like a person being chased along a road, there will be no leisure for careful, focused recitation;
such haste fails to reach the full count. Therefore, know that the expression "one hundred thousand" is a general term used to denote the maximum.
It is the intention of not being separated for even a moment, yet it does not necessarily limit itself to the number of one hundred thousand recitations.

I fear that those who recite the Buddha’s name with faith might cling to this [specific count] and thereby develop a spiritual ailment; therefore, I have cited what I have personally tested to inform you.
Some may say, "This is a matter belonging to the master's state of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), and thus is beyond my knowledge."
Those who travel to famous mountains do not wish to go to the West;
those who travel to Mount Wutai say, "Mañjuśrī is here"; those who travel to Mount Emei say, "Samantabhadra is here"; and those who travel to Putuo... [say, "Avalokiteśvara is here"].
It is said that Guanshiyin is present; yet why is it not also said that in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss there dwells Amitābha?

Furthermore, why is it not said that rather than merely admiring the illustrious names of the Three Great Beings, it would be more beneficial to personally bask in the radiant light of Amitābha Buddha as he currently preaches the Dharma?
Moreover, why is it not said that one need not traverse three mountains over many years and months before arriving? This is indeed [the truth].
To be reborn by merely recollecting the Buddha for the duration of a single finger-snap is truly a matter of great wonder.

Regarding the end of life in the Pure Land, the second vow asks: "Among the devas and humans in that land, when their lives come to an end, none shall ever again be born into the three evil realms. Thus, it is said:
There is birth and there is death; it is simply that one does not fall [into the lower realms]. What is meant by those born in that land all having immeasurable life? Is it not said later:
"The lifespan of the devas and humans in that land is all immeasurable, except for those who, by their original vow, wish to emerge and save sentient beings"?

The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) also states: "Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) upon being born in that land, they return to this world to rescue [beings]."
Regarding suffering sentient beings, he compassionately vows to transform them through his practice; this is not comparable to the cycle of death and rebirth in this world.
He does not aspire for the Western [Pure Land].
Someone once asked a monk, "Do you wish to be reborn in the Western [Pure Land]? He replied, "I do not wish for that. Rather, what I wish for is to come back to life here."
He wore a robe of fine silk and lived with one wife and one concubine; this, he said, was his own Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When questioned, he remained silent and informed me of this. I remarked, "Each person has their own aspirations. If one's will is set upon wealth and status, why seek the West?
Nevertheless, although wealth and status are not the admirable pursuits of a practitioner of the Way, they must nonetheless be attained by cultivating the merit of worldly fortune."
If one does not cultivate merit, one will not necessarily become a groom for a noble lady, but may instead become a servant who provides her garments.
One will not necessarily be matched with a virtuous woman from a renowned clan, but may instead offer the six rites of marriage to a commoner. Yet even that is not certain.

If one has committed evil deeds, one will not even become a servant providing garments, but may instead become a member of the "Golden-Robed Gentlemen" (the executioners); such matters are not yet settled.
This can be known. Furthermore, one may not be permitted to receive offerings from the people of Qi, yet one might instead find refuge among the grooms, the trainers, or the cooks;
whether this will happen is as yet unknown. It is still not certain. Should one’s karma become heavy, the golden robes may perhaps change into red iron plates;
whether this will happen is as yet unknown. The grooms, the trainers, and the cooks may even transform into *āpādas*.
Thus it is; the matter cannot yet be known. How tragic!
He did not wish for the Western [Pure Land].
Again, he asked another monk, "Do you wish to be reborn in the West? He replied, "I do not wish for it, nor do I not wish for it. [He wished for] the East.
"There is a Buddha; I shall go to the East. There is a Buddha in the West; I shall go to the West. It is the same for the South, North, above, and below.
Why should I be restricted to the West alone? He then asked another monk, "Do you wish to be reborn in the West?
The monk replied, "If the Eight Vajra-Gods carry me to the East, I will not come. If the Four Heavenly Kings carry me to the West, I will [not come]."
I do not go. How could I know what is meant by "east" and "west"? To observe them together: the first person among them is one who is submerged in the five turbidities.
Of these two people, one is subject to birth (*samsāra*), while the other is without birth (*nirvāṇa*).

Nevertheless, although one is said to be subject to birth, it does not necessarily mean that they can truly act as their own master without being dragged along by karma. As for the one said to be without birth, it does not necessarily mean—
Only those who have truly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) abide eternally in the light of quiescence;

if they have not yet reached this, they are merely engaged in frivolous proliferation (prapañca). If they have not even reached that, they are merely shamelessly making grand claims. How difficult this is!
When one recollects the Buddha, one does not see those who have attained awakening;

yet when asked about those who have attained awakening through Zen meditation (*chán*), they appear before our eyes in the records. Why is it that those who have attained awakening through the recollection of the Buddha are so few and rarely heard of?

Alas, there certainly are such people, but you have simply not seen them. Furthermore, as for those who practice Zen meditation, they attain the principle— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.*
Later, he never again spoke boastfully to proclaim himself. Only after being pushed forward by the dragons and devas did his voice resound throughout the age and his fame endure for posterity.
That man of Caoxi, who carried the Heart-Seal of Huangmei, had indeed not let his mouth slip regarding the wind and the banner.
He was merely a hunter guarding a net. Chingsu received the secret transmission from Ciming;
had it not been for their chance encounter at the lychee grove, he would have been nothing more than an old man in a single forest. How could you know him otherwise?

Furthermore, as for those who truly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, their resolve is to depart from Saṃsāra and they seek the Pure Land with such intensity that every thought is like the urgency of saving one's own head from fire. This is precisely what he meant.

To awaken to the Amida of one’s own original nature and to realize that the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is nothing but one’s own mind—if such a person remained hidden throughout their entire life and never emerged from seclusion, how could you possibly know of them?
Those born in the highest of the high grades are all people who have attained awakening; thus, one must not fail to read the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth).
"One miss is a hundred misses," as the ancients said: "If one does not practice in this life, one miss is a hundred misses. From one to a hundred—how many misses there are!
It reaches this point: the Sūtras say that it is difficult to leave the evil realms and obtain a human body; having obtained a human body, it is difficult to encounter the Buddha-dharma.
Nevertheless, encountering the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance and believing in and accepting it is even more difficult.
As stated in the sutras, an ant has not been liberated from its ant-body since the time of the Seven Buddhas;

how can it know on what day it will obtain a human body, on what day it will encounter the Buddha-Dharma, or on what day it will encounter the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance and believe in and accept it? It is not merely a hundred missed opportunities—it is indeed a thousand.
Ten thousand errors, yet they are inexhaustible. How tragic!

To look down with contempt upon the Western layman Bao Shi, who daily recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, until after a long time his understanding and realization became thorough and proficient, whereupon he subsequently composed [the following] regarding the West...

The Discourse on the Directions. This consists of three sections in response to inquiries from visitors. The first section discusses orthodox principles while gradually suggesting that the Western [Pure Land] is insufficient for rebirth.
The subsequent two sections vehemently argue against those who aspire to be reborn in the West. Someone urged me to refute them;
however, I recalled the words of Chan Master Konggu, who likened such erroneous speech to the songs of woodcutters and the chants of herdsmen.
There is no need to debate with him. What Bao has discussed here all cites the correct principles of the Chan school, which are easily used to lead people astray;

thus, he causes sentient beings to fall into doubt and error, causing them to lose their aspiration for rebirth [in the Pure Land]. The harm this inflicts is not slight, and one cannot remain silent forever.
The first chapter is divided into three grades of the Western Land: first, the Western Land produced by Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and other bodhisattvas;
second, the Western Land produced by such spiritual friends as Huiyuan and Yongming, and such worthies as Su Shi and Yang Cigong;
and third, the Western Land for ordinary people, evildoers, and animals.
...and so forth. The claim that the Western Pure Land is produced [by such means] seems plausible at first glance;
however, the nine grades of rebirth are clearly stated in the sutras, as manifest as the sun and moon in the midst of the sky. Why must you wait to establish another threefold classification?
When a single king establishes a law, ten thousand nations revere it; can a commoner of the mountains and fields establish his own ordinances? This is the first error. The Buddha...

Regarding the clarification of the nine grades: originally, there were not two lands in the Western Paradise; however, because the capacities of sentient beings differ, those who attain rebirth therein naturally form these nine grades.
Bao’s assertion—that the West originally possessed three grades of land intended to accommodate three grades of people—does not accord with the sutras;
this is his second error. Furthermore, he states that all past masters and virtuous ones have gone [to the Pure Land].
Birth [in that land] is truly not for one's own benefit, but is purely for the benefit of others.
Now, as for seeking birth in that land, it is precisely for the purpose of drawing near to the Tathāgata and aspiring for supreme benefit. Let us set aside for a moment the great Bodhisattvas;

how could even those such as Śrīmitra and Yaśas have all reached the final stage of a Bodhisattva, having gone specifically to Sukhāvatī to save sentient beings while no longer seeking their own benefit? (From the Verses of the Chapter on Vows and Practices)

He said: "I personally beheld the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light and saw him bestow upon me the prediction of Bodhi before my very eyes. To seek this prediction is nothing other than for one's own benefit;

this is the third error. Furthermore, he said: 'The Sage and the ordinary person share the same essence; it is only through delusion and awakening that their superiority and inferiority are temporarily distinguished.'"
"Reflecting back and turning the light [of awareness] around—this is as simple as turning over one's hand—and yet the distinction between the holy and the ordinary becomes vast.

Now, if it is through this reflection that they become so vastly different, can you say their essence is the same? To do so would contradict your own words; this is the fourth error. Furthermore, you say:

'Do not cling to the mark of self if you wish to be born in that land,' yet the Buddha repeatedly exhorted and warned us to aspire for birth there. This means the Buddha is teaching people [to seek rebirth]."
"To cling to the mark of a self is the fifth error. As for the second and third sections, they are even more disparaging, and their errors are even more severe.
They say: 'Those who currently preside over the Dharma take only the Pure Land as their concern; they take only this matter as the truth.'"
If so, is the Pure Land then false? Is the Buddha’s teaching on the Pure Land a deceptive lie?
To disbelieve in the existence of the Golden World is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* rebukes. That Bao recites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* daily yet holds such a nihilistic view is his sixth error.
Furthermore, it is said: "Single-mindedness without distraction" does not refer to the mere act of holding the name while remaining focused on every thought-moment.

If one speaks of "holding," there are as many examples as clouds; I have personally seen several individuals who recited the Buddha's name day and night and were even certified by several senior spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Yet, later they all fell into the snares of Māra and could not be rescued. Indeed, regarding the holding of the name, the Buddha—

This is indeed so. Is it that the Buddha has mistakenly caused these people to enter the snare of Māra? We currently see those who do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) but instead engage in Chan meditation, yet still become possessed by demons.
Why is this? The sutras state that those who attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha will never fall back and will certainly enter the stream of the sages (*ārya-srotas*).
Since the Buddha permits entry into the stream of the sages, for Bao to claim they instead enter the snare of Māra is his seventh error. Furthermore, he says:
What is called "single-mindedness" (ekacitta) is precisely the mind inherently possessed by each person. It is primordially numinous and wondrous; it is primordially complete.
Apart from this, there is no other dharma. Now, the sutra text clearly states: "Uphold the Name with single-mindedness, without distraction.
How can one discard the four characters of the preceding phrase and speak only of "single-mindedness"? Without the authority of the sutra text, to speak so loftily with empty words—
Discourse. Thus, it is not incorrect to say that the mind is also non-existent; this is the true speech and the actual speech uttered from the Golden Mouth.
Is this the Buddha’s definitive teaching, or has Bao altered it? The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "With single-mindedness, invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, how can this be explained? This is the eighth error. Again, it says: "If one practices according to this dharma, one will inevitably enter a deviant path.
Previously it was said that one enters the snares of Māra; now it is said that one enters a deviant path. Is the harm caused by *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) such as this?

Why did the Buddha not forbid people from reciting the Buddha's name, waiting instead for [your] prohibition like that of Baozhi? This is the ninth error. Furthermore, it says: "The ancients of old first exhorted people..."

One attains the fundamental [realization] first, and only afterwards is one exhorted to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Now, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth is originally a matter of "ascending to the ultimate through the preliminary study.

Is it logically sound to first achieve ultimate realization and only then engage in preliminary study? Could there ever be one who has already attained the rank of Chief Minister after passing the imperial examinations as a top graduate, yet only then begins to study the Six Classics, the *Analects*, and the *Mencius*, or to compose the literary essays required for the civil service exams? Such an error would be tenfold.
Furthermore, it is said: "If the Buddha-dharma were limited to this, a single scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* would suffice.
Relying solely on this sūtra, who could not become a teacher of devas and humans? Who could not be called a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend)?

Now, as for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other such Mahāyāna sūtras—there is no day they are not recited, and no day they are not expounded. Who, then, is it that... [is partial]?

"Do you hold fast to the single sutra of Amitābha and thereby sweep away all other sutras? Nevertheless, I fear it is simply that you have not yet truly relied upon this one sutra with exclusive devotion.
If by relying exclusively on one sutra one attains the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (nien-fo san-mei), what disgrace would there be in being called a 'Good Spiritual Friend' (kalyāṇamitra)?
This is the eleventh error. Furthermore, he says: "The Buddha-fields are infinite. If one were to teach people exclusively to seek rebirth in only one field..."
"Are the other Buddha-fields not tranquil and cool? How could one know that all sentient beings, as numerous as atoms, are born within a single field without it appearing to increase?
Or that not even a single being among those as numerous as atoms fails to be born in that field, yet it does not diminish?
What is cold and what is warm? What is still and what is noisy? To harbor such childish views and heterodox doctrines is the twelfth error."
Throughout thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises, the Western Land is praised; thousands of sages and ten thousand worthies have sought rebirth in that realm.
That you alone, Master Bao, should so severely disparage it—how can you not fear the karma of your speech? When you first began, your faith was devout and sincere;
I held you in great esteem. Now that you have become like this, I am deeply concerned for you.
There are three types of filial piety:

the great filial piety that transcends the world and the filial piety of the world. Regarding the filial piety of the world, there are two: first, attending to one’s parents with joy and serving them with fine food and drink;

second, attaining the civil service examinations and entering officialdom to honor one’s parents with rank and emolument. As for the filial piety that transcends the world, there is one: [namely, the attainment of the Way].

Parents. Third, by cultivating virtue and exerting oneself in practice, one becomes a sage or a worthy person to bring glory to one's parents. These three constitute what is known as filial piety in the world.

As for filial piety that transcends the world, it involves exhorting one’s parents to observe the fasts and uphold the Way, to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land, thereby forever parting from the four modes of birth and bidding eternal farewell to the six realms of existence, so that they may entrust their essence to the womb of the lotus flower. Parents...
Beholding Amitābha, one attains non-retrogression; thus, for a filial son to repay his parents, there is nothing greater than this.
In the past, when I first began to enter the Way, both my parents had already passed away. I composed a "Text on Mourning My Own Filial Failure" to express my grief and resentment.

Now, seeing both laypeople and monastics among the assembly who possess the joy of having both parents living, my sentiments of sorrow increase all the more, and tears flow freely from my eyes and nose.
I prostrate myself and bow my head to offer this exhortation.

Regarding the question of one person concerning the difficulty of purifying the Pure Land: Śākyamuni Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe, and it immediately became a world of golden color. The Buddha was fully present.

If such supernormal powers exist, why not immediately transform this Sahā world—this place filled with impurities, earth, stones, and mountains—into the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with the seven treasures?
Why must sentient beings necessarily be made to traverse the vast distance of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands?
Alas! The Buddha cannot save those who lack the karmic affinity; do you understand this, Subhūti? Pure.
One attains the Pure Land through causal conditions. If the minds of sentient beings are impure, although the Pure Land exists, by what means could they be born there?
It is like the case where practicing the ten wholesome deeds leads to rebirth in heaven, such that even hell is transformed into paradise;

yet those sentient beings who commit the ten unwholesome deeds cannot, even with the Tathāgata extending his golden arm to pull them, cross its threshold even once. Therefore, in a single kṣaṇa, the golden world—
The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and it remained as the Sahā world once more. Again, a person asked:

"The sutras state that a single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha with a sincere heart extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. Does this statement refer to a literal fact?"
Is this logic? Alas, the Sūtra says: "A single invocation of 'Namo Buddha' has already established one upon the path to Buddhahood. It further says:
"In a single prostration to the Buddha, from the heels of the feet up to the Diamond Realm (Vajrapada), every speck of dust represents the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

Now, there is truly no need to debate whether these matters accord with principle; one must simply apply oneself to the two characters for "sincere mind" (*zhìxīn*). One’s only concern should be the state of the mind.
"It will not be reached. Do not worry that your transgressions will not be extinguished. As it is with phenomena, so it is with principle; as it is with principle, so it is with phenomena.

Why should you have any doubt? Furthermore, one person asked: 'There is someone who has diligently practiced mindfulness of the Buddha throughout their entire life, yet at the moment of death they experience a single thought of regret and consequently fails to attain rebirth.
Conversely, there is someone who has accumulated evil throughout their entire life, yet at the moment of death they resolve to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.'"
Thus, they attain rebirth in the Pure Land. If this is so, why would the virtuous suffer loss, while the wicked, conversely, reap benefit?
Alas! Among ten thousand people, there is but one who, having accumulated evil throughout their life, maintains right mindfulness at the moment of death.
Were it not for the roots of goodness planted in previous lives, how could one possibly give rise to such a state when overwhelmed by the agony of death, falling into a state of stupor and confusion?
Are you truly mindful? It is only one in ten thousand that regrets at the moment of death;
even if such a case occurs, it must be someone who practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name with indolence throughout their life, rather than one who was diligent.
Diligence means the mind is free from distraction; perseverance means the mind is without interruption. How could regret arise in such a person? Such [regret] is the result of having committed evil.
Those who are thus situated should urgently cultivate self-reflection; do not harbor deluded thoughts that such a stroke of luck might occur at the moment of death.
Those who sincerely seek the Pure Land should simply increase their own diligent efforts; do not worry about falling back or regretting at the time of death.
Regarding the practice of counting beans while reciting the Buddha’s name for the sake of patrons who have made offerings: for every single recitation of the Buddha’s name, one passes a bean.
One person initiates this, and others follow suit; they are known as "Bean-Buddha Masters. Indeed, when the World-Honored One taught people to recite the Buddha’s name, he established [this method].
"This is being used as a rosary. Why do you not follow the Buddha’s regulations by performing tasks that save effort instead of engaging in this laborious task?
Furthermore, with a rosary of one hundred and eight beads, once they are exhausted, one begins again; even up to hundreds of thousands, millions, or billions, they are inexhaustible.
Now, with these beans joined together, once they are exhausted, one likewise begins again and they are also inexhaustible. Why then do you discard the beans that have already been counted?"

Do not use it anymore; replace it with something new. Their statement says: "Even if one counts [the beads] up to a *dou* or a *shi*, and sends them to various hermitages and temples to provide offerings of fermented beans for the assembly, this too is a detour.
Someone may say: "There were those in antiquity who practiced this, as recorded in the *Ōjōshū* (Collection on Rebirth).

[The author] replies: They did not count the beans themselves; bystanders calculated their recitation of the Buddha’s name, which was so vast it could not be measured. This is merely an approximation.
"Two full years" refers to this very period. Now, large grain ships carry a thousand *shí* of rice; "two years' worth" is merely a way of speaking to emphasize the great quantity.
It does not mean they count individual beans as people do today. Even if one were to actually count the beans, their minds would still not be like those of people today.

Regarding the question of whether those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) should maintain a single mind without distraction, Miaoxi said: "Fools spend their entire days counting beads in pursuit of pure karma;
is the practice of *nien-fo* truly the act of a fool? Alas! I have previously debated this matter. Miaoxi merely stated that fools spend their entire days counting beads...
Zhuhong sought pure karma; he did not say that a fool who maintains a single-minded state without distraction throughout the day seeks pure karma.

He further cited a verse by an ancient worthy which says: "Those who attain Buddhahood are rare, yet those who recite the Buddha’s name are many; if one recites for a long duration, it may instead result in demonic influence.

If you now wish to easily attain Buddhahood, a mind free of recitation is no less effective than much recitation. This is "reciting the Buddha’s name without recitation. How can this be achieved with a mind possessed of [conceptual] existence?
To say "be mindful of the Buddha at every thought" is an exhortation for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha with a distracted mind and fail to observe the mind itself.

It does not mean that after a long period of time, one who achieves a state where the mind is undisturbed becomes a demon. Never having practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, they first worry about the occurrence of such mindfulness.
